text: An N x N optical multiplier performs N^2 MACs per pass but pays only O(N) conversions at its edges. If the interface tax is about 5 pJ per input-output sample pair, why do small arrays (N = 8) lose before the light is even turned on?
choices: Because small arrays have intrinsically higher optical loss per MAC
Because the laser wall-plug efficiency falls at small N
Because the per-MAC interface energy is E_tax/N: about 78 fJ/MAC at N = 64 but 625 fJ/MAC at N = 8 — worse than a mobile NPU
Because small arrays cannot use wavelength-division multiplexing
explanation: The conversion tax amortizes as E_tax/N, so a 5 pJ tax gives 625 fJ/MAC at N = 8 (worse than a digital NPU) but only 78 fJ/MAC at N = 64. Choice 0 confuses optical loss with the interface tax; choice 1 is not the mechanism (WPE does not scale this way with N); choice 3 is a real limit but not why the amortization math fails at small N.
